headline: Housing market conditions vary significantly by state, with WA and SA having a 12-month pipeline buffer while Melbourne continues to struggle
reasoning: Reardon highlights that Australia effectively has a dozen or more distinct housing markets driven by state government and local council policies. Western Australia and South Australia builders have roughly 12 months of sold-but-not-commenced homes in their pipeline, acting as a significant shock absorber against the current downturn. Melbourne is at the other extreme, having struggled to recover from the previous cycle even after three RBA rate cuts, and faces additional uncertainty from a state election later in the year that further dampens buyer and builder confidence.
quote: Look we have a dozen maybe 20 different markets around the country. We're back to that situation where state government policies, local council policies are what is driving the volume of homes at each individual region. Western Australia and South Australia both have a builders. There would have maybe 12 months worth of work in the pipeline of homes sold that they haven't yet commenced. So there's a big shock absorber there. The case the other extreme is certainly Melbourne. We have seen Melbourne really struggle to come out of the last cycle. Those previous three cuts to the cash rate weren't sufficient to get that market going. They do have the added uncertainty of a state election later this year. And those do. Those people don't buy and you don't build a new home unless they're confident about their own employment.
episode_title: Home building is hitting the brakes

headline: Reardon expects house price decline to be relatively shallow and short-lived given strong underlying demand from low unemployment and migration
reasoning: Despite the policy headwinds and confidence shock, Reardon argues that fundamental demand drivers — low unemployment and strong migration — remain robust and will ultimately bring buyers back to the market. Rental vacancies are tightening weekly and rental prices are rising, which he views as better indicators of underlying supply-demand than spot house prices. He expects the price decline to be shallow (5–10%) and short-lived, potentially ending by late 2025 or early 2026, with that magnitude only taking prices back to levels seen 12–18 months prior.
quote: We suspect it's going to be relatively shallow and probably not long lived. And that's because demand for housing, whether it's through today unemployment's and remains very low, that creates demand for housing. Migration is another factor that creates demand for housing, both of which are very strong. So we're going to see demand for housing growing. We're seeing each week rental vacancies are getting tighter, rental prices are rising. And that's a much better measure of underlying supply and demand equation than retail prices on any given week. So given that those fundamentals remain strong within a very short period of time, households are going to have to get back to making decisions about their life, where they want to live, in the type of home they want to live in, and we're likely to see a relatively short decline in home prices, whether it's over by the end of this year or early next year, probably isn't going to be the big driver and the depth of it a 5% decline, even a 10% decline, is only going to take home prices back to where they were 12 to 18 months ago, depending on which market you're looking at.

headline: Reardon does not expect interest rate cuts in the near or medium term, with elevated government spending keeping unemployment low and inflation sticky
reasoning: Reardon argues that government expenditure remains elevated, which is keeping unemployment very low and in turn keeping inflation figures elevated. This dynamic makes it unlikely that the RBA will ease rates anytime soon — he specifically says a rate cut appears unlikely even this year. Consequently, a meaningful recovery in new home construction and home prices is unlikely until the cash rate is cut, which he sees as a medium-term rather than near-term prospect.
quote: Our concern is that unemployment is very sticky. We're seeing unemployment remain very low, and it's remaining low because the government expenditure remains elevated. And while we have elevated expenditure, low unemployment. Those inflation figures are probably also going to remain elevated. So I'm not sure that we're going to see an easing in interest rates anytime soon. Certainly this year it appears unlikely. And so yes, it's likely that we won't see a substantial growth in home prices and therefore a substantial pickup in new home building until we see a cut to the cash rate. But I think that's unlikely in the short term or even in the medium term.
episode_title: Home building is hitting the brakes

headline: SMSF policy change described as one of the worst own-goal housing policies in recent years, removing a key source of new supply without dampening demand
reasoning: Reardon argues the government's decision to remove SMSFs from investing in new homes is counterproductive: SMSFs don't live in houses so the policy will not reduce demand, but it will reduce supply by approximately 3,500–5,000 detached homes and a similar number of apartments annually. The government also stands to lose roughly half a billion dollars per year in federal revenue from detached housing alone. He characterises this as one of the worst own-goal housing policies seen in recent years, with no clear public benefit.
quote: The long term consequence, though, of the changes to negative gearing capital gains tax will be a negative for new home building, but the one that we're particularly concerned about, one that is a really sharp attack on building of new homes, is the policy around self-managed super funds? Quite why the government has sought to remove self-managed super funds from building new homes isn't clear what the motivation, what the benefit to the public of that policy isn't clear. They're certainly going to lose about a half $1 billion per year in federal government revenue just from detached housing alone. And we're also likely to see three and a half, 5000 fewer detached homes built every year, probably a similar number of apartments not built every year. And of course, given that self-managed super funds don't live in houses, it's not going to have any impact on demand for houses. So one of the worst own goal housing policies that we've seen in recent years overall.
episode_title: Home building is hitting the brakes

headline: HIA's Tim Reardon warns budget policy changes have caused a broad pause in new home construction across all buyer segments
reasoning: Reardon notes that recent budget decisions — including changes to negative gearing, capital gains tax, and self-managed super fund (SMSF) rules — have created policy uncertainty that has caused all buyer types (investors, owner-occupiers, first home buyers) to withdraw from the market. Data from inquiry and display-site visit numbers show a fall-away in every market. The SMSF policy in particular is described as a 'sharp attack' on new home building, likely resulting in 3,500–5,000 fewer detached homes and a similar number of apartments per year, while costing the federal government around $500 million in annual revenue. The negative gearing/CGT changes are expected to result in roughly 35,000 fewer homes over the decade, moving Australia further from its 1.2 million home target.
quote: What's happened in the market is that everybody has paused. It's not just investors pausing and withdrawing from the market. It's not just owner occupiers first home buyers. The uncertainty that these policy decisions have created has caused all buyers just to retreat back. So we can see from the data that we don't publish that number of people visiting displaced sites, a number of leads and inquiries that are coming through a fall away in every market.
episode_title: Home building is hitting the brakes
